k-1.x_notes: Six concise problems at actual size, touching both kernels. P1 has six well-chosen boards: hexagon, 2x2 parallelogram and chevron work; side-2 triangle, 3-triangle trapezoid and an even-area 1-3 trapezoid (5 up, 3 down) do not. It asks children to X and say why, which is the obstruction idea at entry level. P2 asks for fewest greens on side-2/3/4 triangles (2, 3, 4). P3 is 'find all the ways' on the 1-hexagon (2 ways, 3 copies) and the 2,1,1 hexagon (3 ways, 4 copies), worded correctly. P4 asks for fewest blocks with five block types (answers 3, 3, 4). P5 is a placement game on 4/5/6/7-triangle strips and a hexagon, with varied answers (first, second, first, first, second). P6 finds all 6 tilings of the 1,2,2 hexagon. That is plenty of real work and not dumbed down. Weaknesses: drawing rhombi on the half-size copies in P6 is hard for kindergartners; 'say why' and 'be sure to win' need adult support; there is little recording scaffolding for non-readers.
k-1.y_notes: A K-friendly font, yes/no circles and 'How many?' boxes make it easy to use. P1 has four boards, including the even-area 2-4 trapezoid that cannot be covered, but asks no 'why'. P2 matches X. P4 asks for fewest blocks on T3, a side-2 hexagon and T4 (3, 6, 5). P5 asks children to build the big shapes from small blocks of the same color: green and red work, yellow and purple do not. This is a lovely concrete task. The game has tally boxes for who won, a nice concrete record, though both strips are 'first wins'. Weaknesses: P3 says to cover each copy 'in a different way', but every shape has one more copy than it has tilings (3 copies for 2 ways, 4 for 3, 5 for 4), so the stated task cannot be completed and could mislead the parent volunteer. Page 4 is an unlabeled continuation, page 7 is mostly blank, and the shared rules are wordier.
k-1.reason: Both are substantial and concrete. X's problems are precisely worded, with a richer contrast set in P1 and a 'why'. Y has a charming rep-tile problem, but its main 'find the tilings' problem asks for more different ways than exist, which would confuse a non-mathematician adult.

grades-2-3.x_notes: This band is tightly sequenced and covers kernel 1 fully in 7 pages. P1: the star works (6 forced rhombi), T3 fails on odd area, the 2-4 trapezoid fails with even area, and the 2,1,1 hexagon works. P2: a hexagon with two same-color holes fails. The bowtie is balanced, but its two halves are not, so it fails. A hexagon with one up hole and one down hole works (verified). P3: T2-T5 need 2-5 greens, with an explanation for T5. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100. P5 compares chevrons with blues on the same triangles in a table and asks why chevrons can never do better. P6: invent a connected 20-triangle board that needs 6 or more greens (it can be done). P7 is an open investigation: where can two greens go on the side-2 hexagon? I checked all 144 up/down pairs, and every one works, so the rule is clean and provable. Writing lines are included. Weaknesses: 'explain' recurs often, and P4 has no physical component.
grades-2-3.y_notes: This band is also strong, with correct mathematics, at 11 pages. P1: a side-2 hexagon and the 2x chevron work; T3 and T4 do not (T4 has even area). P2 (T3-T5) and P4 (a large T7 with explanation) repeat the same triangle task. P3 gives four fixed hexagons with two triangles removed: the up/down pairs work and the same-color pairs do not (verified). It is the closed version of X's open P7. P5 compares chevrons on T3, T4 and T6, though the blue count for T6 was never done earlier. P6 is excellent: two balanced 18-triangle boards that still need 2 and 4 greens because of local imbalance. P7 asks for the smallest board that needs 3 greens (7), a good optimization. Weaknesses: more pages and page-turning, the repeated triangle problems, no generalization to large n, and wordier rules.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are mathematically sound and rich. X develops the idea more efficiently, from concrete boards to generalization (10, 100) to an open rule-finding investigation, in fewer pages. Y's bottleneck boards are a real plus but do not outweigh its repetition.

grades-4-5.x_notes: This band covers all of kernel 2. P1 asks for the 6 tilings of the 1,2,2 hexagon. P2 adds flips and a flip graph (maximum distance 4). P3 asks for fewest flips for three pictured pairs on an actual-size side-2 hexagon. P4 asks for round trips of 4, 5 and 7 flips. P5 defines ribbons clearly with a worked picture, and states that the side-2 hexagon has two ribbons, which is exactly the tool needed for flips. P6 asks for proofs of the parity and of a lower bound. P7 counts the 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon, with 25 copies. P8 counts the 1,3,3 hexagon (20). Weaknesses: P2 makes children redraw all six coverings again, and P7 needs about 20 more drawings, so there is a heavy drawing load. P6 is a standalone proof-only page of the kind the organizer keeps with adults. Ribbons are applied to counting only once (P8).
grades-4-5.y_notes: This band also covers all of kernel 2, with better development. P1 has a graded entry: A (2 ways), B (3) and C (6), with half-size copies clearly marked for drawing. P2 builds a flip map using numbers, so there is no redrawing, with a fill-in for the maximum. P3 defines chains, asks whether a covering is unique given its chain, and asks what a flip does to the chain. P4 counts the 1,2,3, 1,3,3 and 1,4,4 hexagons (10, 20, 70, verified), which builds toward binomial counting. P5 prints the start covering on actual-size boards, numbers the flip points 1-7 so children can record their flips, and asks for a lower bound on c. P6 asks for round trips of 4 and 6 flips and whether an odd round trip is possible. P7 counts the side-2 hexagon. The pictured coverings I checked are valid. Weaknesses: chains are defined only for hexagons one edge wide, so the parity and lower-bound arguments on the side-2 hexagon need the adult to extend the idea. P7 has no drawing copies, and F (70) is a stretch.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are substantive. Y's concrete recording tools (printed start boards, numbered flip points, a numbered map) and its counting sequence 6, 10, 20, 70 give children more thinking and less redrawing. X's two-ribbon setup is a cleaner path to the parity proof.

overall.reason: The packets are close in quality and both are mathematically correct. X is more concise and precisely worded in the two younger bands, and its 2-3 sequence ends in a strong open investigation. Y's main K-1 tiling task asks for more ways than exist. Y has the better 4-5 band, but the margin there is small.
